fields.label: Background — why are we here?
fields.prompt: A focused, concise paragraph giving an overview of the CURRENT brief: the business problem or opportunity and enough relevant context to understand why the brief exists and why now (2–3 sentences). Plain words, no jargon. If there's no marketing strategy behind it, there's no brief yet.
fields.good_example: Sales have plateaued and under-35s see us as 'their dad's beer.' A low-carb variant launches in Q3 — our one shot to feel relevant to a younger drinker.
fields.bad_example: We want a big, disruptive campaign that goes viral and builds brand love.
fields.bad_reason: States a wish for advertising, not the business problem; no 'why now'.

rubric.test: Within the word limit (brief is brief).
Describes a business problem/opportunity, not an ad request.
Makes the timing clear.

fields.label: Objectives (commercial · behavioural · attitudinal)
fields.prompt: State what this brief is here to achieve. Lead with ONE primary objective, in the level that matters most; the other levels are supporting and only as far as they help it. Commercial = the business result; behavioural = what people must DO; attitudinal = what they must think/feel first. Each measurable and time-stamped where the input allows.
fields.good_example: Commercial: +8% volume share in 18–34s within 12 months. Behavioural: 100k under-35s trial the variant. Attitudinal: from 'beer for older men' to 'beer for people like me.'
fields.bad_example: Increase awareness, sales, loyalty and consideration.
fields.bad_reason: Multiple unranked objectives, none measurable or time-bound; awareness is not a commercial outcome.

rubric.test: All three levels present (commercial, behavioural, attitudinal).
Commercial objective is measurable and time-bound.
The three levels form a logical chain.

fields.label: Audience — one human
fields.prompt: A targeted, specific and succinct picture of the people the work is aimed at, built ONLY from the brief's data, with their relevant motivations, situation and behaviour (not generic demographics): who they are (demographics), what they think, feel and want (psychographics, needs), how and where they use the product, and who the brand is NOT for. Keep every audience the brief names, in priority order (primary / secondary); a B2B audience is a buying group, not a person. A group written in a pen-portrait voice is fine. Never invent a named person, an age, a city or habits the brief does not give. Avoid clichés like 'millennials'.
fields.good_example: Busy (working) mothers. A 'Life is Sweet' / 'food is love' family where mum tends to over-feed everyone. She keeps the fridge well stocked as family meal-times can be erratic.
fields.bad_reason: A bare data cell: 'Adults 18-64 really doesn't help the creative team' (Weichselbaum p.304). Nothing about how they think, what they want, or who is excluded. The opposite fault is as bad: a named person with an age, a city and habits the brief never gave.

rubric.test: Within the word limit.
A vivid picture from the brief's data: demographics, psychographics and needs or wants (not a bare data cell) — and NOT an invented individual with an age, a city or habits the brief does not give.
Says who the brand is NOT for, or which audience comes first when the brief names several.

good_examples: Busy (working) mothers. A 'Life is Sweet' / 'food is love' family where mum tends to over-feed everyone. She keeps the fridge well stocked as family meal-times can be erratic.

Primarily, disaffected mid-corporate customers of other banks: companies with a turnover of between £1m and £130m p.a. We are talking to the owners/directors. Secondarily: existing customers and staff.
fields._example_sources: Cadbury's Chocolate Trifle brief, BBH, 24 Jan 1995 (BBH 1995 upload, slide 11); NatWest Mid Corporates brief, BBH, 10 Feb 1995 (slide 17). R2 §5.2: all 16 legible BBH audience boxes describe a group; none names a person. Third-party upload, not independently authenticated.
fields._rubric_sources: BBG p.16 ('a vivid picture of demographics, psychographics and needs or wants'), BBG p.10 ('equally clear on who it is not'); replaces is_human, which passed only invented personas and failed every faithful extraction incl. the B2B employer brief (R2 §3.2, audit H4)

fields.label: Budget & scope
fields.prompt: The money, and the honest ambition it buys. Budget ↔ objectives ↔ audience are linked — move one and the others must move. State whether the budget includes VAT and whether media sits inside it; if the brief does not say, ask the client (an open question) rather than assuming. Never state a budget figure that was not given.
fields.good_example: €1.2m working media. National reach unrealistic — prioritise four cities + always-on social.
fields.bad_reason: No constraint = the backbone can't be balanced.

rubric.test: States a real budget/scope constraint.

fields.label: Competitor context
fields.prompt: Who are we up against, what does each rival claim (their positioning and messaging), and what space has no rival claimed? Needed to judge whether the single thought is ownable.
fields.good_example: Rivals all claim heritage, mateship and 'the perfect pint.' White space: nobody owns 'the drink that signals your taste.'
fields.bad_reason: No real category read; can't locate white space.

rubric.test: Names rivals and the shared category claim.
Does it name the space no rival has claimed (a messaging gap or opening), not only who the rivals are?

fields.label: The insight
fields.prompt: A truth about the audience, usually a human tension, that when said out loud makes them feel understood and gives the product a role to play. A surprising, meaningful discovery the client did not already know (cultural, personal, human or industry-based), grounded in evidence rather than obvious statements. Not a fact, a statistic or an observation. Reveal WHY, not just WHAT. Shape: 'They [do/believe X] because [deeper motivation], which means [implication].' Survive the 'so what?' test ×3.
fields.good_example: Buyers don't reject the Fabia on its engineering — they reject it because 'it's still a Skoda', which means the job is to confront the prejudice, not to prove the car.
fields.bad_reason: An observation about the product with no motivation and no implication; the creatives' answer was 'Yes, but it's still a Skoda' (Fallon 2006 p.77).

rubric.test: Within the word limit.
States a motivation (look for 'because'), not only a behaviour.
Contains an opposing force / tension.
Survives three 'so what?' probes.
Is it true, and would the audience nod and feel seen?
Is it about the audience, not a boast about the brand or a fact about the product?
Is it fresh, not a category cliche anyone could have written?
Does it hand the product a role? Says what the job actually is. An insight that does not set up the proposition is just a nice observation.

fields._example_sources: Built from Fallon 2006 pp.77-80 (Skoda Fabia, Fallon London 2000): 'the biggest barrier was an irrational prejudice against the brand' (p.80); the good example's wording is ours, its facts are the source's. IPA case: 'It's a Skoda. Honest.' reduced marque rejection from 60% to 42%.

fields.label: Single-minded proposition
fields.prompt: The single most motivating thing we can say to the defined audience, given the insight and what is honestly true about the product: ONE thought, not a thought with an 'and': a word, a phrase or one sentence, never several thoughts. It must follow from the problem and the insight, be true and backed by the reasons to believe, give this audience a reason to care, and be specific to this brand, not a category generic. Written for the creative team: it points to where the idea should be and is not the idea's final wording. Not a tagline, not 'creative', not a list. If you have two, choose, or find the higher thought that contains both.
fields.good_example: A smart choice because you don't pay for what you don't need.
fields.bad_example: Good drinks, fun times, real people.
fields.bad_reason: 'It is not a main idea, but three main ideas' (Steel 1998 p.169); averaged from research, it 'could have fitted any one of a host of other beverages' (p.89).

rubric.test: One sentence at most: a word, a phrase or one sentence is fine; several sentences are several thoughts.
Within the word limit.

One thought, not a thought with an 'and': does it commit to one thing to communicate, rather than joining two claims for the creatives to choose between? If it has an 'and', does the 'and' join two thoughts (fail) or sit inside one thought (pass)? Two clauses joined by a colon, semicolon or dash also count as two thoughts.
Would a reader who has read only the problem and the insight see why this is the proposition?
Is it true: supported by a reason to believe the brief actually holds?
Is it a plain statement of the thought: no pun or double meaning, no hype standing in for a thought, and not the brand's sign-off line? (Being short, or able to run as a headline, is NOT a fail.)
Not a category generic: most rivals could not say it just as well. (A pre-empted claim that no rival currently makes counts as specific. Needs competitor_context.)
Would this audience care? Is it motivating to them, not merely true or unique? (An emotional reason counts.)
Could a creative team write several quite different ads from it?

fields._prompt_sources: R1 2026-09-24 §1.1: Steel 1998 p.168-169; APG 1997 pp.56-57; BBG p.17; Excellence 1997 p.158; Reeves 1961 p.47; benefit not required (Ogilvy DO, BBH 1992 slide 32, Binet & Field 2007)
fields._word_limit_note: 3-20 is our convention as a sanity limit; no source sets a number (R1 C13)
fields._rubric_sources: R1 §3: C1 Steel p.169/APG p.56; C2 Excellence p.158, Steel p.169, BBG p.17; C4 BBG p.17, BBH 1992 slide 9, Steel p.149 (headline-able is not a fail); C6 APG p.57, Steel p.169; C7 Reeves p.48, Weichselbaum p.305, Binet & Field 2007; C8 Reeves p.47, Trott 2022, RSE 2007/Sharp 2010 (keep soft); C10 Excellence p.158. 'tolerance: hard' = a fail is final regardless of the gate's one-fail tolerance
good_examples: A smart choice because you don't pay for what you don't need.
Häagen-Dazs is the ultimate sensual intimate pleasure.
contrast_examples: Proposition: 'Renting from Granada is more sensible than owning.' — Copy: 'Why buy a millstone when you can rent a milestone?' (Excellence 1997 p.159; the same support sits under both)
Proposition: 'the picture is only the beginning' — Line: 'See What Develops' (Steel 1998 pp.174-175, Polaroid)
Convergence is allowed: 'Levi's 501s are the original and definitive jeans' ran with the sign-off 'The Original Jeans' (BBH 1995 slide 14)
fields._example_sources: E2 Motel 6, Weichselbaum p.305; E1 Jose Cuervo, Steel 1998 p.169 (bad) — 'A party waiting to happen' (good); E9 Häagen-Dazs, BBH brief 10 Feb 1995 (BBH 1995 slide 16). Page numbers for Steel/Excellence verified by wording 2026-09-25, not by page (T8).

fields.label: Reasons to believe
fields.prompt: The few validated facts, truths, statistics or sound logic that directly support the proposition: strongest first, not a shopping list. Validate the premises: logic does not replace empirical proof for a factual or product claim. Never invent supporting evidence; a reason you cannot prove from a fact starts 'To confirm:'.
fields.good_example: You can stay always up to date · Nicam · widescreen · satellite
fields.bad_example: Award-winning · trusted · premium · loved by thousands · refreshing · bold.
fields.bad_reason: Generic, unprovable claims; a shopping list, not proof for the SMP.

rubric.test: No more than five items.
Every item supports the SMP.

fields._example_sources: Granada TV Rental support, Excellence 1997 p.159 (Duckworth): 'If you rent from Granada you can stay always up to date. Nicam, widescreen and satellite'. Replaces the invented '3g carbs / blind taste test' line (audit H1: the style example was itself an invented stat).

fields.label: Desired response (think · feel · do)
fields.prompt: The intended behavioural, attitudinal or other response to the work, clearly tied to the brief objectives: the meaningful change or action we want. One line each.
fields.good_example: Think: 'this one's actually for me.' Feel: quietly proud to order it. Do: ask for it by name at the bar.
fields.bad_reason: Vague; 'engage' is not an observable behaviour and doesn't ladder to the objective.

rubric.test: Think, feel and do all present.
'Do' ladders up to the behavioural objective.

fields.label: Tone, world & distinctive assets
fields.prompt: Personality in ~3 words + the distinctive assets that must carry through every execution (logo, colour, character, sonic, line). Set the world; don't prescribe the idea.
fields.good_example: Dry, confident, never try-hard. Always: the red flash, the 'O,' the two-note sound sting.
fields.bad_example: Make it a cinematic hero film with a celebrity.
fields.bad_reason: Prescribes the execution; that's the agency's job, not the brief's.

rubric.test: Sets a world without prescribing the creative idea.

fields.label: Mandatories & practicalities
fields.prompt: What's genuinely fixed — deliverables & channels, key dates, budget constraints, legal must-haves, and anything to AVOID. Keep tight; detail → appendix.
fields.good_example: 3×30s + 6s cutdowns + OOH + social. Responsibility message required. Live 1 Sept. Don't reference competitors.
fields.bad_reason: No fixed deliverables, dates or constraints to plan against.

rubric.test: Lists concrete deliverables or constraints.

fields.label: The job — what must this work make a person do?
fields.prompt: The job in ONE plain sentence, from the audience's side: the business problem reframed as the change in what ONE person thinks, feels or does. Not the task ('make an ad'), the problem ('nobody under 35 thinks of us'). Words a normal person would say out loud.
fields.good_example: Get a tired thirty-year-old to think of us first when a plain Tuesday dinner needs lifting.
fields.bad_example: Launch a 30-second TV and social campaign to drive awareness.
fields.bad_reason: States the task, not the problem or the change in a person (strategic-planning skill: reframe the problem from the audience's side).

rubric.test: Exactly one sentence.
Within the word limit.
Does it state the problem or the change that is needed, not the task the client asked for?
Is it written from the audience's side, naming the change in what one person thinks, feels or does?
Is every word one a normal person would say out loud?
Does it name ONE change in ONE person, not several asks joined together?

fields.label: The barrier — what stands in their way?
fields.prompt: What stands between this person and the result right now: the belief, habit, fear or rival in their head or routine, in plain words. The strategy usually lives in removing one barrier. Rest it on what the brief holds, or mark it to confirm.
fields.good_example: They file the jar under 'my mum's cupboard', and nobody browses their parents' pantry.
fields.bad_reason: A symptom a tracker measures, not what is in their heads or habits (strategic-planning skill: the barrier is in their heads or habits).

rubric.test: Within the word limit.
Does it name a belief, habit, fear or rival in the audience's head or routine, not a media, product or sales fact?
Does it name ONE barrier rather than a list of them?
Is every word one a normal person would say out loud?

fields.label: The objection — the doubt the single thought must beat
fields.prompt: The doubt already in the audience's head that the single-minded proposition has to beat, in their own words. The work answers it; it does not ignore it. ONE sentence.
fields.bad_example: People may not know about the product.
fields.bad_reason: A gap in awareness, not a doubt the audience actually holds.

rubric.test: Exactly one sentence.
Within the word limit.
Is it a doubt this audience actually holds, in their words, not a gap in awareness?
Does the single-minded proposition answer this doubt rather than ignore it?
Is every word one a normal person would say out loud?
Is it ONE doubt (one worry in one sentence), not two or three joined together?

open_questions.prompt: What we don't know, what we assumed, and what to ask the client. Auto-populated whenever a field is 'missing' or confidence < floor.

criteria.prompt: How will we judge the work? Agree the shared criteria BEFORE creative starts. (Only ~30% of brands do — cheapest way to avoid endless rounds.)

gate.note: A brief becomes a contract only once the agency accepts it.

definition_of_done.rule: Exactly one strategy. Two messages → two briefs.
All required fields present for this brief_type.
SMP is one sentence within the word limit.
Evaluation criteria agreed before creative starts.
No field exceeds its word limit.
Brief sets the problem; it does not prescribe the idea.

dependencies.rule: Budget ↔ objectives ↔ audience must be mutually realistic.
The SMP follows visibly from the problem and the insight (the derives_from check).
Judging 'ownable' needs competitor_context; without it the check is left for review, not failed.

positioning_statement.label: Brand positioning statement
positioning_statement.template: FOR [audience] WHO [need], [BRAND] IS THE [frame] THAT [benefit] BECAUSE [RTB]; UNLIKE [competitor], [BRAND] [differentiator].
